title: Tarantino Surprises AFI Fest With First 17 Minutes of Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Sequel
excerpt: Quentin Tarantino surprised AFI Fest on Oct. 23 by screening the first 17 minutes of 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,' written by him and directed by David Fincher.
content:
Quentin Tarantino gave a Hollywood audience something no trailer has: the first 17 minutes of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. At AFI Fest on Friday night, October 23, after a screening of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood at the TCL Chinese Theatre and a question-and-answer session, Tarantino surprised the crowd by rolling the opening of the sequel instead of just talking about it, according to Deadline and TheWrap.

"I could talk more about 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' or I could show you the first 17 minutes," Tarantino told the audience, according to TheWrap. He chose the second option.

The film is written by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher. Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth, the role that earned him the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the 2019 original. The sequel picks up in June 1977, eight years after the original film's 1969 setting.

According to TheWrap's eyewitness account of the footage, Cliff has seemingly left stunt work behind and is now working as a manager at the New Beverly Cinema in Los Angeles, the theater Tarantino owns. The opening includes a film-within-the-film, "Soul Brothers Die Hard," featuring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Peter Weller as Cliff's father, a pawn shop owner. The footage also shows Cliff buying stolen items, including a Best Director Oscar, before the action escalates.

The story follows Cliff as a Hollywood fixer, solving problems for people in the entertainment industry. The cast also includes Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan and Carla Gugino, among others. The film is set for IMAX theaters on November 25, before its Netflix debut on December 23. The 17-minute preview itself has not been publicly released.

Analysis: A Handoff, Not a Reunion Tour

What makes this preview notable is not just its secrecy, but its authorship. Tarantino wrote the sequel to his own film and then handed the director's chair to Fincher, a filmmaker with a very different, colder precision. The footage described so far leans into that contrast: a 1977 Los Angeles built from repertory-cinema detail, a fixer who no longer needs to be a stuntman to be dangerous, and a hero whose workplace is a movie theater. If the full film sustains that tone, it will not feel like a nostalgia exercise. It will feel like Tarantino's mythology filtered through someone else's discipline, arriving first in IMAX — a deliberate bid for theatrical scale before it becomes a streaming title. For audiences in Laredo and across the border, the December 23 Netflix date is the one that matters most, but the November theatrical window is the signal that Netflix still believes this one deserves a big screen first.
